title: fix-network features
description: What the tool offers: separate health per dimension, an explanation of each failing internal host, an outcome for every finding, adaptive repair, the Wi-Fi watchdog, the after-sleep hint, the run's record and the JSON report.

entities.name: Health per dimension
entities.description: Seven dimensions, each reported on its own: local network, public internet, VPN connection, routing, corporate DNS, corporate service and proxy.
entities.behavior: Each dimension gets one of HEALTHY, FAILED, NONE, UNKNOWN, NOT TESTED or UNSUPPORTED with a one-line detail. A check that did not run is NOT TESTED, never HEALTHY. Healthy public internet does not make the VPN healthy. The run is healthy only when no dimension is FAILED.
entities.outcome: The person sees which layer is broken, and that a working internet says nothing about the VPN or the intranet.
constraints: Corporate DNS is NOT TESTED without a host-name --internal-host; corporate service is NOT TESTED without a HOST:PORT.
A tunnel whose client scutil does not manage is UNSUPPORTED: observed through its routes, its state unreadable.
When the local network has failed and the public probes fail too, public internet is FAILED without a finding of its own.

entities.name: Why an internal host fails
entities.description: For each --internal-host, the report says which of five causes it is.
entities.behavior: The host is resolved through the system resolver and, when that fails, asked of the matching split-DNS server (or the primary one) directly with dig. The report then says whether the name does not resolve (server down, no split DNS from the VPN, or the local resolver at fault), resolves to 0.0.0.0 or loopback, is routed around the tunnel, fails TCP through the tunnel, or the service itself is down.
entities.outcome: The person learns whether to reconnect the VPN, flush DNS, check a DNS filter or /etc/hosts, or ask whoever runs the service.
constraints: When public DNS is failing too, a failing internal name gets no finding of its own; the public DNS finding covers it.
A TCP failure gets no finding of its own when there is no IP path to the internet, or when the host is already reported as routed around the tunnel.
The direct query needs dig; without it a local resolver fault cannot be told apart, and the failure is put down to the DNS server or the missing split DNS.
Routing around the tunnel is judged only for private, carrier-grade NAT or unique-local addresses while a tunnel carries routes.

entities.name: An outcome for every finding
entities.description: Every finding ends as fixable, not fixable by this tool, or reboot needed.
entities.behavior: A fixable finding lists its steps and, in a diagnosis, the exact fix command line with the flags it needs. A finding the tool cannot fix says what to do instead. A reboot is offered only where it is the known fix: configd hung, Wi-Fi hardware missing or a radio that will not power on, a system resolver that still fails after a flush while the server answers directly, and stale routes or split-DNS resolvers that outlive the VPN client. Once a finding's steps have all been tried, it falls back to its manual or reboot advice. The report ends with whether a Wi-Fi reset is required.
entities.outcome: The person (or an agent relaying it) knows the next action for each problem without interpreting the checks.
constraints: In fix, a step that was not run is reported as 'fixable but not run', or 'fixable but not allowed' with the flags to add.

entities.name: Adaptive repair, least disruptive first
entities.description: fix runs one allowed step at a time, re-checks, and stops as soon as everything is healthy or nothing more is allowed.
entities.behavior: Steps are ordered turn Wi-Fi on, flush DNS, clear the gateway ARP entry, disable unreachable proxies, reconnect the VPN, renew DHCP, cycle Wi-Fi, flush routes. Each round assesses a fresh snapshot, runs the first allowed step not yet tried, and takes a new snapshot. With --force the standard ladder (flush DNS, clear ARP, renew DHCP, cycle Wi-Fi, where they apply) runs first. When any step ran, the tool waits 15 seconds and verifies every dimension again, internal hosts included. Every command's exit status, and any networksetup error text, decides whether the step is ok or FAILED.
entities.outcome: The network is repaired with as little disruption as the evidence allows, and the final report shows whether it worked.
constraints: Wi-Fi is cycled only for a local-link or upstream fault, never for a VPN-only fault.
Each step runs at most once per run.
Gated steps need their flag; over SSH, disruptive steps need --allow-remote.
A VPN reconnect stops it if needed, waits up to 8 polls of 2 seconds for Disconnected, starts it and waits up to 15 polls for Connected.

entities.name: Wi-Fi watchdog
entities.description: Before cycling the radio, a detached script is started that turns Wi-Fi back on after 45 seconds.
entities.behavior: recover.sh is written to the run's state directory and started in its own process group. The log names its pid and the manual rescue command for the device. If the radio comes back on, the watchdog is stopped; if not, the step fails and the watchdog still turns Wi-Fi on and logs that it did.
entities.outcome: A Wi-Fi cycle cannot leave the Mac (or a remote session) without Wi-Fi.
constraints: If the watchdog cannot be started, the Wi-Fi cycle does not run.

entities.name: After-sleep hint
entities.description: VPN-related findings within an hour of waking from sleep say how long ago the Mac woke.
entities.behavior: The wake time from sysctl kern.waketime is compared with the clock; findings whose codes start with vpn-, corp- or stale-, and internal-route, get '[woke from sleep N min ago: a stale VPN session is likely]'.
entities.outcome: The person is pointed at a stale VPN session as the likely cause.
constraints: Only within 3600 seconds of the wake (RECENT_WAKE).

entities.name: A record of every run
entities.description: Each run keeps its log and the settings it found in a private, timestamped state directory.
entities.behavior: Before any change, the tool creates the directory (mode 0700), and saves original.json: the active service's addresses, DNS servers, search domains, proxies, PAC URL, interface and Wi-Fi power, the routing table, scutil's DNS, proxy and VPN lists, and a summary of the snapshot. Every printed line also goes to diagnostic.log. Lines that look like they assign a password, passphrase, secret, token, PSK or private key are dropped from both.
entities.outcome: What the network looked like before any change, and everything the tool did, can be read afterwards.
constraints: The tool never deletes old run directories.
The original settings are recorded, not restored automatically.

entities.name: Machine-readable report
entities.description: With --json, the terminal output is replaced by one JSON document for the whole run.
entities.behavior: The document holds whether the run is healthy, every check, every finding with its code and remedy, whether a Wi-Fi reset is required, the plan with what blocks each step, the actions and their results, a summary of the snapshot, and the paths of the log and the state directory.
entities.outcome: Scripts and agents can parse the result instead of the text.
constraints: The log still receives every line; errors before the report go to stderr.
